results.content: # How to Measure Spatial Model Performance: Key Geospatial Evaluation Metrics. In the field of geospatial data science, assessing the performance of spatial models is crucial for ensuring the accuracy, reliability, and generalizability of predictive models. Whether you are developing land cover classification models, object detection systems using satellite imagery, or spatial interpolation tools for environmental modelling, using robust evaluation metrics is essential to quantify performance and inform improvements. ## Why Spatial Model Evaluation is Unique. Useful for segmentation or object detection models (e.g., road detection, building footprint extraction):. * Measures the spatial overlap between predicted and ground-truth objects. * High autocorrelation in residuals implies the model may be missing spatial patterns. Cross-Validation Strategies for Spatial Models. Evaluation of spatial models involves more than just great accuracy; it also involves reliable, comprehensible, and spatially resilient validation. Practitioners may make sure models function well not only statistically but also spatially and operationally by selecting the right combination of accuracy, error, object-based, and spatial correlation metrics.

Bring the best of human thought and AI automation together at your work. # Adjusting classification thresholds based on test set predictions. I have a binary classifier that was trained using k-fold cross validation. I then use the model to get predictions on an unseen (held out) test data set. For my specific application, I would like a certain recall value at the expense of a lower precision by varying the probability threshold - e.g. if the predicted probability is above 41%, predict 1, else 0 (rather than the default 50%). Is it ok to choose this probability threshold **based on the predicted probabilities of the test set?** Or would this be considered biasing the model and not generalizing to new data? If the latter, how could I choose a probability threshold that achieves my desired recall score (using the training data perhaps)? ## 1 Answer 1. You can set the threshold on any set of hold out data you'd like, but that set of data then indeed incurs an optimistic bias about your performance metrics. Generally you want to hold out either a third validation set (not recommended for smaller datasets, due to high estimation variance), or use some nested cross-validation/bootstrapping technique to work out the proper threshold. ## Your Answer. Different users/stakeholders might care about different performance metrics (eg overall accuracy vs F1 score). In a main text table summarizing model performance, would it be acceptable to report metrics for different thresholds? (i.e., report F1 for the threshold that maximizes F1, report accuracy for the threshold that maximizes accuracy; note thresholds are chosen in the validation set and performance would be reported on the test set). On the other hand, the very fact that different KPIs (F1, accuracy etc.) are optimized by different decision thresholds points to a graver underlying problem. I argue here and here that this reflects that fact that thresholding an (often implicit) probabilistic classification is the same thing as taking an *action* or a *decision* based on the classification. And evaluating this thresholded decision via accuracy or F1 etc. Such an evaluation only makes sense if we take both the probabilistic classification *and* the costs of our decisions into account: a false positive incurs different costs if it means sending a marketing email to someone who will delete it versus diagnosing a bone cancer that means we need to amputate a leg. disagree based on which threshold is chosen means that they optimize for different costs of true/false positives/negatives (and in the decision framework, I consider talking of "positives" and "negative" misleading, see below). not) based on your probabilistic classification and the true state of the world (your recipient's being interested in your product, your patient's truly having cancer), then optimize the threshold, and then report the resulting cost. In addition, consider that there may be more than one decision, and more than one threshold, based on a given probabilistic classification: a high probability of cancer means that we should amputate immediately before it spreads further, a medium probability means we should run more tests, and a low probability means that the patient is fine. Yes, it is acceptable to report performance at different thresholds in the main text, provided it is clearly stated that these thresholds are chosen based on validation data, and the purpose is to explore the model’s potential.
